A side handle for a hand-operated power tool comprises a handle rod, a fastening mechanism, and a damper. The handle rod is intended to be gripped by a user during operation of the power tool, while the fastening mechanism serves to attach the side handle to the tool in a releasable manner. The damper is arranged between the handle rod and the fastening mechanism so that vibrations transmitted from the power tool to the handle rod can be reduced.

The fastening mechanism is designed to secure the side handle to the power tool by means of a tensioning band and an associated tensioning mechanism. The tensioning band can be placed around a corresponding receiving portion of the power tool, for example around a collar or housing section. By actuating the tensioning mechanism, the tensioning band is tightened, thereby clamping the side handle securely to the power tool. When the tension is released, the side handle can be removed or repositioned.

The tensioning mechanism includes a displaceable collar, a pull rod anchored to the tensioning band, and a rotatable tensioning wheel. The pull rod is connected to the tensioning band in such a way that displacement of the pull rod changes the effective tension in the band. The pull rod is provided with an external thread, which is engaged by the rotatable tensioning wheel. When the tensioning wheel is turned, its engagement with the external thread causes the pull rod to move axially. This axial movement tightens or loosens the tensioning band, depending on the direction of rotation.

The damper connects the handle rod to the fastening mechanism and includes a leaf spring. The leaf spring is configured to absorb or attenuate vibrations occurring during operation of the power tool. In particular, the leaf spring has an inclined longitudinal side, which may influence its spring characteristics and allow controlled elastic deformation between the fastening mechanism and the handle rod.

The leaf spring also includes a slot extending along the handle axis. A splint fastened to the pull rod engages in this slot. This engagement can guide or limit relative movement between the pull rod and the leaf spring while still permitting elastic deflection of the damper. As a result, the side handle can be firmly attached to the power tool while reducing the transmission of vibration to the user’s hand.
outputs.L4:
A side handle for a hand-operated power tool is designed to provide both secure attachment to the tool and improved vibration damping during operation. The handle includes a tool mount that can be fastened to a housing or collar portion of the power tool by means of a releasable fastening mechanism. This fastening mechanism includes a tensioning band that can be placed around the mounting region of the tool, a pull rod connected to the tensioning band, a tensioning wheel for tightening or loosening the pull rod, and a collar that supports and guides the fastening components. By rotating the tensioning wheel, the user can draw the pull rod into tension, thereby tightening the tensioning band around the tool. This allows the side handle to be fixed firmly in a desired angular position and, when required, released again for repositioning or removal.

The side handle also includes a handle rod intended to be gripped by the user. In order to reduce the transmission of vibration from the power tool to the user’s hand, the handle rod is not connected rigidly to the tool mount. Instead, a damper is arranged between the handle rod and the mount. This damper provides an elastic and vibration-absorbing coupling, so that shocks and oscillations generated during drilling, hammer drilling, chiseling, or similar operations are at least partially isolated from the hand grip. As a result, user comfort is improved, fatigue is reduced, and the tool can be guided more accurately over longer periods of use.

A key feature of the design is the use of a slotted leaf spring as part of the damping and coupling arrangement. The slotted configuration allows the leaf spring to flex in a controlled manner under load while still maintaining sufficient stiffness for stable handling. The slots influence the spring characteristics and help define the direction and extent of elastic movement between the handle rod and the tool mount. This enables the side handle to absorb vibration without making the grip feel loose or unstable.

The pull rod of the fastening mechanism is guided by a splint or pin arrangement, which ensures reliable positioning and controlled movement of the rod during tightening and release. The splint-guided pull rod helps prevent twisting, misalignment, or unintended disengagement of the tensioning band. This contributes to a robust and easy-to-operate fastening system, allowing the user to clamp the side handle securely to the power tool with minimal effort.

In use, the side handle can be placed around the desired mounting portion of the power tool, adjusted to a comfortable angular position, and tightened by turning the tensioning wheel. The tensioning band then clamps the handle mount firmly to the tool. During operation, the damper and slotted leaf spring reduce the transfer of vibration from the tool to the handle rod, while the fastening mechanism maintains a secure mechanical connection. The combination of an adjustable tensioning band clamp, a guided pull rod, and a resilient damping connection provides a side handle that is both practical and ergonomic.

Overall, the design improves the handling of hand-operated power tools by combining reliable, releasable attachment with effective vibration reduction. The user benefits from a handle that can be quickly mounted, adjusted, and removed, while also offering greater comfort and control during demanding work.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in communication. It is called a definite article, and it helps us point to something specific. For example, when we say “a book,” we could mean any book. But when we say “the book,” we are talking about a particular book that the speaker and listener both understand.

Although “the” may seem simple, it brings clarity and precision to language. It helps identify people, places, objects, and ideas. Phrases like “the sun,” “the world,” and “the truth” feel definite and meaningful because of this small word.

In writing, “the” often guides the reader’s attention. It tells them that something is known, important, or already mentioned. Without it, sentences can sound unclear or incomplete. For such a short word, “the” has a powerful effect on how we understand meaning.

In many ways, “the” shows that even the smallest words can have great importance.

counterfactuals.output:
## European Patent Claim Summary — Hand-Operated Power Tool Side Handle

### Independent Claim — Side Handle Assembly

A side handle assembly for a hand-operated power tool, comprising:

- a fastening device configured to releasably secure the side handle assembly to a housing, neck, collar, or mounting portion of the power tool;
- a handle grip for manual support of the power tool;
- a threaded pull rod operatively connected to the fastening device;
- a tightening wheel arranged on the threaded pull rod and rotatable by a user to axially displace the pull rod, thereby tightening or releasing the fastening device; and
- a damping connection arranged between the fastening device and the handle grip,

wherein the damping connection comprises at least one leaf-spring damper, the leaf-spring damper having a longitudinal slot extending in a length direction of the leaf-spring damper, such that vibrations transmitted from the power tool to the handle grip are reduced while mechanical support forces are transmitted through the side handle assembly.

### Possible Dependent Claim Features

1. The side handle assembly of claim 1, wherein the fastening device comprises a clamping band, clamping ring, or split collar configured to surround a mounting neck of the power tool.

2. The side handle assembly of claim 1 or 2, wherein rotation of the tightening wheel in a first direction draws the threaded pull rod axially to reduce a diameter or spacing of the fastening device.

3. The side handle assembly of any preceding claim, wherein the tightening wheel is arranged coaxially with the threaded pull rod.

4. The side handle assembly of any preceding claim, wherein the tightening wheel is manually accessible from outside the handle grip.

5. The side handle assembly of any preceding claim, wherein the leaf-spring damper is arranged between a fastening-side support member and a grip-side support member.

6. The side handle assembly of any preceding claim, wherein the longitudinal slot divides the leaf-spring damper into two resilient spring limbs.

7. The side handle assembly of any preceding claim, wherein the longitudinal slot has closed ends.

8. The side handle assembly of any preceding claim, wherein the longitudinal slot extends substantially parallel to a longitudinal axis of the handle grip.

9. The side handle assembly of any preceding claim, wherein the leaf-spring damper is made of spring steel, fibre-reinforced plastics material, or another resilient material.

10. The side handle assembly of any preceding claim, wherein the leaf-spring damper is configured to flex in response to vibration components transverse to the longitudinal axis of the handle grip.

11. The side handle assembly of any preceding claim, wherein the damping connection comprises two or more leaf-spring dampers arranged in parallel or on opposite sides of the threaded pull rod.

12. The side handle assembly of any preceding claim, wherein the threaded pull rod extends at least partially through or alongside the damping connection.

13. The side handle assembly of any preceding claim, wherein the tightening wheel is located between the handle grip and the fastening device.

14. The side handle assembly of any preceding claim, wherein the handle grip is mounted to the leaf-spring damper by at least one screw, rivet, pin, or overmoulded connection.

15. A hand-operated power tool comprising a housing and a side handle assembly according to any preceding claim, wherein the fastening device secures the side handle assembly to the housing or to a mounting neck of the power tool.

### Concise Claim Essence

The invention concerns a side handle for a hand-held power tool in which clamping to the tool is achieved by rotating a wheel on a threaded pull rod. The handle grip is vibration-isolated from the fastening portion by a leaf-spring damper provided with a longitudinal slot, allowing resilient deformation and vibration attenuation while maintaining a robust mechanical connection.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe the construction and operation of a detachable auxiliary handle for a drill or hammer drill, using formal patent terminology and reference numerals for each part.
counterfactuals.output:
A detachable auxiliary handle assembly **(10)** for a hand-held power tool, such as a drill or hammer drill **(12)**, comprises a grip portion **(14)**, a clamping arrangement **(16)** configured to be removably secured to a tool housing or collar **(18)**, and a tightening mechanism **(20)** operable by the user to selectively lock and release the handle assembly **(10)** relative to the tool **(12)**.

The auxiliary handle assembly **(10)** includes an elongate handle body **(22)** having a proximal end **(24)** and a distal free end **(26)**. The handle body **(22)** preferably defines an ergonomic gripping surface **(28)**, which may include ribs, grooves, or a resilient overmold **(30)** to improve manual engagement and vibration damping. The proximal end **(24)** is connected to, or formed integrally with, a clamp support portion **(32)**.

The clamping arrangement **(16)** comprises a generally annular clamp band **(34)** defining a receiving opening **(36)** sized to surround a cylindrical or substantially cylindrical mounting portion **(38)** of the drill or hammer drill **(12)**. The clamp band **(34)** may be split to define opposed clamp ends **(40, 42)** separated by a gap **(44)**. The clamp ends **(40, 42)** are movable toward and away from one another to vary the effective diameter of the receiving opening **(36)**.

The tightening mechanism **(20)** includes a threaded fastener **(46)** extending through aligned apertures **(48, 50)** in the opposed clamp ends **(40, 42)**. The threaded fastener **(46)** cooperates with a threaded nut member **(52)**, threaded insert, or internally threaded portion formed in one of the clamp ends. A manually actuatable tightening knob **(54)**, wing element, or rotatable sleeve is coupled to the threaded fastener **(46)** so that rotation of the tightening knob **(54)** causes axial displacement of the clamp ends **(40, 42)** relative to one another.

In one embodiment, the handle body **(22)** itself serves as the tightening knob **(54)**. The handle body **(22)** is mounted for rotation about a longitudinal handle axis **(56)** and is operatively connected to the threaded fastener **(46)**. Rotation of the handle body **(22)** in a first direction draws the clamp ends **(40, 42)** together, thereby reducing the diameter of the receiving opening **(36)** and clamping the auxiliary handle assembly **(10)** onto the mounting portion **(38)**. Rotation in an opposite direction permits the clamp ends **(40, 42)** to move apart, releasing the clamping force and allowing removal or angular repositioning of the handle assembly **(10)**.

The clamp band **(34)** may include an inner bearing surface **(58)** adapted to engage the mounting portion **(38)** of the tool **(12)**. The inner bearing surface **(58)** may be provided with a friction liner **(60)**, elastomeric pad, or serrated engagement formations **(62)** to resist rotational slipping during operation, particularly during hammer drilling. The tool mounting portion **(38)** may include complementary ribs, flats, or indexing recesses **(64)**, and the clamp band **(34)** may include corresponding indexing projections **(66)** to permit selective angular positioning of the auxiliary handle assembly **(10)** around the tool axis **(68)**.

The clamp support portion **(32)** may further include a boss **(70)** or yoke structure receiving the proximal end **(24)** of the handle body **(22)**. A washer **(72)**, bushing **(74)**, or thrust bearing may be positioned between the handle body **(22)** and the clamp support portion **(32)** to facilitate rotation during tightening while maintaining axial load transfer. A stop member **(76)** may be provided to limit loosening travel of the threaded fastener **(46)** and prevent unintended separation of the tightening mechanism **(20)** from the clamp band **(34)**.

In use, the operator loosens the tightening mechanism **(20)** by rotating the tightening knob **(54)** or handle body **(22)** in the release direction. The receiving opening **(36)** is thereby enlarged sufficiently to permit the clamp band **(34)** to pass over or around the mounting portion **(38)** of the drill or hammer drill **(12)**. The auxiliary handle assembly **(10)** is then moved to a desired axial and angular position relative to the tool housing **(78)**. The operator subsequently rotates the tightening knob **(54)** in the locking direction, causing the threaded fastener **(46)** to draw the opposed clamp ends **(40, 42)** together. The clamp band **(34)** compressively engages the mounting portion **(38)**, thereby fixing the handle body **(22)** in the selected orientation.

During drilling or hammer drilling operation, the auxiliary handle assembly **(10)** provides a secondary gripping point spaced from the primary tool handle **(80)**. Loads imparted to the handle body **(22)** are transmitted through the clamp support portion **(32)** and clamp band **(34)** into the tool housing or collar **(18)**. The friction liner **(60)** and/or indexing formations **(62, 66)** resist undesired rotation of the handle assembly **(10)** relative to the tool **(12)** under torque reaction and vibration. When removal is desired, the tightening mechanism **(20)** is loosened until the clamping force is relieved, after which the auxiliary handle assembly **(10)** may be detached from the mounting portion **(38)** without requiring separate tools.

Thus, the detachable auxiliary handle assembly **(10)** provides a selectively attachable, angularly adjustable, and manually lockable support handle for improving control of a drill or hammer drill **(12)** during high-torque or percussive operation.
